items.topic: Why energy trading differs from other financial markets
items.definition: Energy trading is distinguished from other financial markets by the difficulty and expense of storing and transporting energy products, which breaks the usual link between current and future prices.
items.core_idea: In most financial markets, buy-and-hold arbitrage ties spot and future prices together, since you can buy today, store, and resell later. Energy products are hard or costly to store and must compete with a continuous new supply, so this link is weak or absent, producing cyclical rather than arbitrage-linked pricing.
key_points: Energy trading consists of both physical cash-market exchanges and forward markets, with most activity occurring in forward markets.
Energy products cannot be substituted across time or location — electricity in one place/time is a different product from electricity elsewhere or at another time.
Financial techniques from other markets (dynamic hedging, risk aggregation) must be modified because energy risks at different locations/delivery dates cannot be aggregated the same way.
Because storage/transport must be arranged in advance, most energy trading is really trading of agreements to deliver in the future, not trading of the physical commodity itself.
relationships: Underlies why spot prices in one location (e.g., Chicago in a cold snap) do not reflect availability or expectations elsewhere, since undeliverable supply has no value to that market.
trading_implications: Traders cannot rely on cash-and-carry arbitrage to keep forward and spot energy prices in line the way they would for storable financial assets.
Location and delivery time are core contract terms, not incidental details, when structuring energy trades.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming energy prices behave like storable-commodity or financial-asset prices, where present and future prices are tightly linked by arbitrage.

items.definition: A trading market allows both buying and selling of a commodity; a cash market may only allow buying, with no ability to resell.
items.core_idea: Not every place a commodity changes hands is a trading market — the defining feature of a trading market is two-way (buy and sell) capability, such as at a service station where gasoline can be bought but not resold.
key_points: Trading = buying, selling, and exchanging commodities, products, and services.
A cash-only purchase (e.g., gasoline at a service station) is not a trading-market transaction because it can't be reversed/resold.
relationships: Distinguishes trading markets from the spot/cash market discussed later in the chunk
trading_implications: Determining whether a venue is a true trading market matters for whether a position can be exited, not just entered.
common_misunderstandings: Conflating any cash purchase with participation in a trading market.

items.topic: Non-storability and immediacy of energy delivery
items.definition: Electricity and heat generally cannot be stored or transported without advance arrangement, and physical energy purchased today usually must be consumed immediately.
items.core_idea: Energy has no intrinsic value in isolation — it is only valuable at a specific place and time (e.g., heat has no value in summer, and gas that can't reach Chicago during a cold snap has no value there regardless of price), so spot prices reflect only what is locally deliverable, not broader future expectations.
key_points: Home heating value is seasonal/contextual — worthless (or negative, i.e., people pay for cooling) in summer.
During a regional price spike (e.g., Chicago cold snap), gas that cannot physically be delivered there has little value, illustrating location-specific worth.
Spot prices in a location reflect current local deliverable supply/demand, not expectations of future prices, because customers cannot defer urgent consumption needs.
Consumers can't relocate overnight to escape a local shortage or price spike.
relationships: Reinforces the non-substitutability point about location/time in energy trading
trading_implications: Local spot price spikes should not be read as signals about future or other-location prices.
common_misunderstandings: Believing that a high spot price in one location implies availability or value of the same commodity held elsewhere.

items.topic: Law of Demand and Law of Supply
items.definition: The Law of Demand states higher prices reduce demand; the Law of Supply states higher prices increase production.
items.core_idea: Traders generally model prices as set by the intersection of supply and demand, with a free market gravitating toward the price level where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
key_points: Theoretically, the supply/demand intersection sets the 'fair' price for an asset.
In practice, supply and demand don't always respond to price changes as theory predicts.
relationships: Foundation for the elasticity concept and inelastic-market price disruptions described next
trading_implications: Basic supply/demand framing is a starting point for price analysis but must be qualified by elasticity considerations in energy markets.

items.definition: Elasticity measures how much supply and demand respond to price changes; when they don't respond ('inelastic'), prices can spike or crash sharply rather than adjusting smoothly.
items.core_idea: In an inelastic market, prices skyrocket when demand exceeds supply and crash when supply exceeds demand, because quantity doesn't adjust to absorb the imbalance — both events are common in energy markets.
key_points: Energy supply and demand are often constant/unresponsive to price changes in the short run, causing price disruptions instead of smooth equilibration.
Price spikes and price crashes are both described as fairly common occurrences in energy markets.
relationships: Directly follows from the Law of Supply/Demand; explains why theoretical equilibrium often fails to hold in energy
trading_implications: Traders should expect sharper, more volatile price moves in energy markets than in markets with elastic supply/demand response.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming energy prices will smoothly equilibrate the way textbook elastic-market prices do.

items.topic: Lag between high prices and new energy supply
items.definition: There is a substantial delay between a price increase and a corresponding increase in energy supply, because new supply requires long-term capital investments (wells, refineries, power plants).
items.core_idea: Because building new energy infrastructure takes significant time and is only undertaken when a permanent price change is expected (not a short-term spike), the supply side of energy markets responds slowly, contributing to inelasticity.
key_points: New supply investments (wells, refineries, power plants) are long-term capital projects, not short-term reactions to price.
Producers commit to new capacity only if they expect a durable/permanent price change, and construction itself takes substantial time.
Consumers also can't easily substitute away from energy demand — they can't relocate, easily convert vehicles to alternative fuels, or forgo winter heating — making them a largely captive audience.
relationships: Explains the supply-side driver of the inelastic-market/price-disruption dynamic described above
trading_implications: Short-term price spikes should not be expected to induce quick supply responses; capacity additions lag price signals by potentially years.
common_misunderstandings: Expecting new energy supply to come online quickly in response to a price spike.

items.definition: The spot market (a.k.a. cash market) is the market for immediate delivery of a commodity — for energy, this can mean delivery anywhere from about five seconds to one month out — typically involving small-quantity purchases for immediate use.
items.core_idea: Spot trades involve the physical transfer of a standardized quantity of a commodity for a set price 'on the spot,' analogous to buying fast food or flipping a light switch (immediately buying and consuming electricity); electricity spot trading is limited to parties who can deliver or use power right away.
key_points: 'Immediate' delivery in energy spot markets can span from seconds up to about a month, given the practical complexity of delivering some energy commodities.
Spot market participants are typically consumers buying small quantities for immediate use.
Only parties able to physically deliver or immediately use power can trade in the electricity spot market.
relationships: Contrasted directly with the forward market definition
trading_implications: Spot market access for electricity is inherently restricted to physical delivery/use capability, unlike purely financial markets.
common_misunderstandings: Thinking 'spot' delivery always means instantaneous (seconds) rather than potentially up to a month for some energy commodities.

items.definition: The forward market is a financial market in which delivery of a commodity is scheduled for an agreed future point in time, typically at least a month ahead.
items.core_idea: Unlike the spot market's immediate delivery, forward markets let counterparties arrange transactions well in advance of physical delivery, and most energy trading activity occurs in this forward segment.
key_points: Forward market deliveries are typically scheduled at least a month in advance.
Most energy trading occurs in forward markets rather than spot markets (per the chapter's Key Topics).
relationships: Contrasted directly with the spot/cash market definition
trading_implications: Forward markets are the primary venue for arranging energy transactions given the difficulty of short-notice physical delivery.
